rows.title: Background radiation
rows.summary: Radiation has always been part of the natural environment.
steps: Background radiation is radiation that is always in the environment. Most of it is natural.
Radon gas from rock and soil is the main natural source. Cosmic rays and minerals in the ground add more.
Food and water carry some natural radioactive material, such as potassium-40.
The most common human-made source of radiation exposure is medical imaging, such as x-rays and CT scans.

rows.title: Why not go out to look
rows.summary: Staying put protects you more than going out to see or to travel.
steps: Radiation levels decrease rapidly during the first 24 hours, becoming significantly less dangerous.
If officials advise you to evacuate, listen for information about routes, shelters and procedures.
If you have evacuated, do not return until local authorities say it is safe.
Leave early only for an immediate hazard such as a fire, gas leak or building collapse, or when officials say so.

rows.title: Exposure or contamination?
rows.summary: Radioactive contamination can be on or inside a person. Radiation itself does not spread.
steps: Contamination is radioactive material deposited on skin, clothing or anywhere it is not wanted.
External contamination: radioactive material on the skin or clothing.
Internal contamination: it is breathed in, swallowed or absorbed through wounds.
Radiation does not spread or get on or in people. Radioactive contamination is what can be spread.
A contaminated person receives radiation exposure until the radioactive material is removed.

rows.title: Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned
rows.summary: The official first steps in a radiation emergency.
steps: Get inside: if warned of a radiation hazard, go straight into the nearest building and move away from windows.
Stay inside: sheltering usually lasts at least 24 hours.
Stay tuned: follow officials' instructions. A battery or hand-crank radio works if other communication fails.
Stay in the most protective spot for the first 24 hours unless a hazard threatens or officials say it is safe.

rows.title: What makes a good shelter
rows.summary: More walls between you and the outdoors means more protection.
steps: Put as many walls as you can between yourself and the outside, and move away from windows.
The safest buildings have brick or concrete walls.
Underground parking garages and subways can also provide good shelter.
The best spot is a basement or the center of a large building.
Close windows and doors, and turn off fans, air conditioners and forced-air heating that bring in outside air.

rows.title: If you were outside
rows.summary: Officials say to get inside, take off outer clothing and wash.
steps: Remove your outer layer of clothing. It can remove up to 90% of radioactive material.
Take clothes off carefully, so you do not shake loose any radioactive dust. Avoid touching your eyes, nose and mouth.
Take a shower or wash with soap and water to remove radioactive particles from skin and hair.
Do not use household cleaning wipes on skin. Hand sanitizer does not protect against radioactive material.
Unsealed foods that were outside may be contaminated with radioactive material.

rows.title: Myth: exposure makes you radioactive
rows.summary: Being exposed to radiation does not make a person radioactive.
steps: Myth: a person who was exposed to radiation is now radioactive.
What is true: radiation does not spread or get on or in people.
What is true: contamination is what can be spread. A contaminated person is exposed until it is removed.
Radioactive material on skin or clothes, or inside the body, is the concern.

rows.title: Myth: any radiation is deadly
rows.summary: What matters is the dose and how fast it arrives.
steps: Myth: any amount of radiation is instantly deadly.
What is true: acute effects such as burns or acute radiation syndrome need very high doses.
What is true: low environmental levels cause no immediate health effects. Cancer risk rises with dose.
A low dose, or one spread over a long time, carries a lower risk, because the body can repair damage.

rows.title: Myth: KI pills block all radiation
rows.summary: Potassium iodide protects one organ from one kind of radioactive material.
steps: Myth: potassium iodide pills protect you from radiation in general.
What is true: KI protects only the thyroid and only against radioactive iodine.
What is true: it cannot reverse damage already done, and may not give 100% protection.
Take KI only if officials or a healthcare provider tell you to.

rows.title: Myth: microwaves are nuclear radiation
rows.summary: Microwaves and radio waves are non-ionizing. Nuclear radiation is ionizing.
steps: Myth: microwave radiation is the same kind of radiation as nuclear radiation.
What is true: radio waves, visible light and microwaves are non-ionizing radiation.
What is true: ionizing radiation has enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms, which can damage tissue and DNA.
Non-ionizing radiation can make molecules vibrate, but it cannot knock electrons out of atoms.

rows.title: Myth: a plant can blow up like a bomb
rows.summary: A reactor does not explode like a nuclear weapon, but an accident can release radiation.
steps: Myth: a nuclear power plant can explode like a nuclear bomb.
What is true: a commercial power reactor cannot explode like a nuclear bomb.
What is true: its fuel is not enriched beyond about 5%, and an explosive needs much higher enrichment.
A serious accident can still release radioactive material, as the Chernobyl accident did.

rows.title: Potassium iodide (KI)
rows.summary: Take it only if officials say so. It protects the thyroid only.
steps: Do not take KI unless public health or emergency officials or a healthcare provider tell you to.
KI protects only the thyroid. It does not protect other parts of the body.
It protects only against radioactive iodine, not other types of radioactive materials.
Table salt or iodine-rich foods are not a substitute for KI.

rows.title: Time, distance, shielding
rows.summary: Three ways to lower the dose from a radiation source.
steps: Time: limiting the time you are exposed reduces the dose from a source.
Distance: the dose decreases dramatically as you move farther from the source.
Shielding: barriers of lead, concrete or water protect against penetrating gamma rays.

rows.title: What a dose is
rows.summary: How much radiation the body takes in, and how fast, both matter.
steps: Damage depends on the absorbed dose, measured in grays. The effective dose is in sieverts.
The dose rate matters too: it is how fast the dose is delivered.
Effects such as burns are more severe at higher doses and higher dose rates.
Low doses delivered slowly carry a lower risk, because the body is more likely to repair the damage.
